title: US Bifurcation, aging, and job growth are shaping the metro consumer outlook
gist: Oxford Economics argues US consumer spending is increasingly concentrated in high-income, asset-rich households, a bifurcation likely worsened by the inflation shock from the US-Israel war with Iran, while population aging reshapes where and what consumers buy. Sun Belt job-growth metros like Austin lead medium-term spending rankings, Northeast/Midwest metros lag, and recreation and health are the fastest-growing categories.

insights.claim: US consumer spending has become more reliant on high-income, asset-rich households buoyed by equity and housing wealth, while lower-income households have struggled.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Spending is hostage to asset prices; an equity/housing drawdown would hit consumption disproportionately.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics says US consumer bifurcation has likely been heightened by the inflation shock from the US-Israel war with Iran and will continue to influence spending.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Geopolitical energy shock deepens K-shape; favour premium/affluent-facing B2C over low-income exposure.
insights.quote: This bifurcation has likely been heightened by the inflation shock from the US-Israel war with Iran

insights.claim: Although AI-related investment has been a major driver of US growth over the past year, consumer spending remains the backbone of the US economy, per Oxford Economics.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Don't over-index on AI capex narrative; consumption trends still dominate GDP.

insights.claim: As seniors take up a greater share of the US population, where they live and what they buy will matter more for spending growth, with retiree hotspots like The Villages ranking high in medium-term spending growth.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Retiree-heavy metros and senior-oriented categories offer structural B2C growth.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects health spending to be among the fastest-growing US consumer categories over the medium term, supported by seniors.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Supports healthcare services/consumer health exposure on demographic grounds.

themes.theme: Sun Belt vs. Northeast/Midwest metro divergence

insights.claim: Many top US metros in Oxford Economics' medium-term consumer spending growth rankings are those with the strongest job growth prospects, such as Austin, mostly located in the Sun Belt.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Geographic tilt for retail/REIT/B2C expansion toward Sun Belt job-growth metros.

insights.claim: Several Northeast and Midwest US metros are forecast to lag in spending growth due to sluggish employment and population prospects and, in some cases, exposure to the spike in essentials prices.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Underweight consumer exposure concentrated in slow-growth Northeast/Midwest metros.

insights.claim: High-income metros such as San Jose feature toward the top of Oxford Economics' medium-term US metro spending growth rankings.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Affluent tech metros remain strong spending markets thanks to high-income households.

themes.theme: Scale beats growth rate in big metros

insights.claim: Oxford Economics argues slower-growing but very large US metros like Chicago still offer huge spending level gains because of their sheer size.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Don't screen markets purely on growth rates; absolute dollar gains in large metros can dominate.
insights.quote: Slower-growing but large metros should not be dismissed as offering limited opportunities.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics expects discretionary categories such as recreation and culture to record among the fastest US consumer spending growth over the medium term, supported by high-income households.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Leisure/experience spending tied to affluent cohort; sensitive to asset-price wealth effects.
